items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

Being part of rigorous, closely supervised research means people in the South Okanagan have a real voice in what the next generation of care looks like,” said Dr. Linda Grasswick, principal investigator for the study in Penticton. Medical Arts Health Research Group is conducting the study under Health Canada and research ethics oversight. The treatment will explore an investigational form of psilocybin, one of the naturally occurring compounds found in many so-called “magic” mushrooms. Adults living with PTSD in the South Okanagan who would like to learn more can contact the study team confidentially at (888) 490-4320 or visit www.healthresearch.ca. Reaching out does not commit anyone to participate. Those interested will be screened by a doctor to determine whether the study is a safe and appropriate fit. Participants will receive care and support from a dedicated study team throughout, and study-related visits, assessments, and the investigational medication are provided at no cost.

items.title: [utilitydive.com] US orders Michigan coal plant to stay open despite court ruling
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The U.S. Energy Department issued a seventh emergency order requiring the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell coal plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, to keep operating for another 90 days, through mid-February 2027, despite a federal appeals court ruling in September that an earlier order was unlawful. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and maintain reliable electricity supplies; the department cited lessons from Winter Storm Fern and other events during the 2026 Arctic cold period. The plant had been scheduled to retire in May 2025. Michigan and other states, along with environmental groups, challenged the earlier orders, arguing there was no qualifying emergency. The appeals court agreed, and the Energy Department has asked the full court to rehear the case. That request remains pending as the new order takes effect.

The World Meteorological Organization said the oceans store more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system, while atmospheric carbon dioxide continued to rise.

items.content_html:

Reports describe deadly glacier flooding in Nepal and wildfires in Europe. Australia released the text on Nov. 16 for negotiations among nearly 200 countries; it includes competing proposals to “transition away” from fossil fuels or phase them out, but either could be removed before an agreement is reached. The draft also proposes at least $120 billion a year for adaptation in developing countries by 2035. Climate campaigners say it lacks a clear process for advancing fossil-fuel roadmaps and that the proposed funding would cover less than a third of estimated needs. The proposed electricity target has also drawn criticism because the text does not require the added power to come from renewable sources. Negotiators must reach consensus before the summit’s scheduled close on Nov. 20. Australia’s climate change and energy minister and lead negotiator, Chris Bowen, expects further revisions as ministers negotiate the disputed language.

items.content_html:

Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), warned at the United Nations climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, that more than 200 million people living in highly climate-vulnerable communities are at risk of displacement. IOM data show storms, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures and floods forced nearly 30 million people from their homes in 2025. Pope said governments spend billions of dollars on border security while underfunding adaptation measures that could help communities remain in place. She estimated the cost of those measures at about $310 billion, compared with roughly $30 billion in funding so far. She argued that helping communities adapt before displacement occurs is more humane and cost-effective than responding to irregular migration after it begins.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UN climate summit ends without pact as fossil fuel dispute stalls talks
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to resolve disputes over fossil fuels and climate finance. The talks ran about two days past their scheduled close, making COP31 the longest COP conference on record. The final draft omitted an explicit reference to fossil fuels, prompting the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable island states to reject it. The draft referred indirectly to the 2023 COP28 commitment to transition away from fossil fuels but did not spell out a pathway or reaffirm the wording. Oil-producing countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, resisted explicit references to fossil fuels, while poorer countries objected that the proposal did not set concrete funding levels for adaptation. COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen said fossil fuels and finance were the main obstacles; summit president Murat Kurum said he would not put forward a replacement draft. Countries agreed on separate measures, including a program to support workers and communities through the energy transition and a plan to assess adaptation progress. More than 80 countries backed Türkiye’s proposed goal of raising electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, but the goal was not part of an adopted overarching pact. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on possible reforms to the consensus-based negotiating process. The next summit is scheduled for Addis Ababa.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Indianola, Texas a coastal town that was once the second largest port in Texas next to at the time Galveston.In 1956 the port received a shipment of camels as part of the United States Camel Corps experiment to replace horses and mules as the primary work animal for southwestern America.

During the Civil War, it was occupied by the Union army, once in 1862, then again a year later. Part of that regiment later drowned moving from Indianola to Matagorda island.

The island was later hit twice again, this time by hurricanes, in 1876 and 1886. The second hurricane was accompanied by a major fire and also submerged most of the town, killing hundreds.

Now basically no sign of the town is left other than a few plaques (one being a marker of where the courthouse used to be). It is however valued as a great spot for fishing for local trout, redfish and flounder.

items.content_html:

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.content_html:

Daily cannabis use is more common than daily alcohol consumption among Canadian adults under 50, according to a study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. Researchers analyzed responses from 99,920 adults in Statistics Canada’s 2023-24 Canadian Community Health Survey: 5.7% reported daily cannabis use, compared with 5.2% for alcohol and 8.5% for cigarettes. The researchers say daily cannabis use is associated with cannabis use disorder, while smoking cannabis poses risks to lung health. About 68% of daily cannabis users reported smoking cannabis, and 41% said they began daily use after legalization. The study relied on self-reported responses and did not distinguish medical from non-medical use.

A James Webb Space Telescope study identified a possible black hole in the young galaxy MARTA 3887, seen as it was about 12 billion years ago. Its estimated mass is 3.3 million suns—about 2.3% of the galaxy’s stellar mass. Separately, researchers analyzing 257 black-hole mergers found a concentration near 10 solar masses and a shortage between 12 and 16, a pattern consistent with some massive stars collapsing without supernova explosions. The merger study does not directly confirm failed supernovae; researchers say more work is needed to test that explanation.

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal has overturned a $100,000 penalty against social media platform X for failing to delete an intimate image posted without a woman’s consent, ruling that blocking access to it in Canada was a reasonable step under provincial law. The tribunal said the law did not make X liable after it blocked Canadian access to the image, which remained available outside Canada. The decision reversed a September 2025 penalty for failing to comply with an order to delete it. The tribunal accepted X’s argument that requiring worldwide removal could interfere with other countries’ legal systems and cited a 2024 Australian case as persuasive but not binding. Outgoing B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma criticized X’s refusal to remove the image and said governments may need to strengthen laws or pursue legal action. The tribunal also rejected X’s request to require the complainant to pay more than US$100,000 in legal fees.

items.title: [aawsat.com] Jaramana car bombing prompts searches in Druze-majority Damascus suburb
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Security teams in Jaramana searched vehicles and checked surveillance cameras after a car bomb struck a residential area near al-Naseem garage, damaging nearby cars and buildings, according to reports. The blast on Saturday, Nov. 14, killed a man and a girl, according to medical sources cited by Asharq Al-Awsat and Al Jazeera. Reports differed on the number of wounded: Syria’s state television said two people were wounded, while the Interior Ministry reported one. The explosion occurred near a battery-production site in Jaramana, a Damascus suburb with a large Druze community. Syria’s Internal Security Forces cordoned off the area and opened an investigation. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said accounts differed over the blast’s precise location and nature, and verification was continuing. Residents told Asharq Al-Awsat they heard the blast at about 8 p.m. and saw the car burning. Security vehicles arrived within minutes, and streets leading to the site were closed, with access allowed for ambulances and civil defense crews.
